opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest shift for me has been moving away from focusing on the most extreme end of the capability spectrum, the wildly superintelligent systems, and towards what I'd call the "early transformative" regime. That's AIs that are powerful enough to be really useful, maybe capable enough to substantially speed up AI R&D or do a lot of the work that human researchers currently do, but not so far beyond us that we have no hope of catching them if they're misbehaving.

A few years ago, a lot of the AI safety community's thinking implicitly centered on the question: how do you align an arbitrarily powerful superintelligence? And that's a really important question, but it's also one where I think it's hard to make concrete progress, and it's not obviously the most decision-relevant one right now.

The reason I've shifted is roughly this. First, I think a big chunk of the risk comes during this intermediate period. If AI companies are deploying very capable models internally, giving them lots of affordances, letting them write code and run experiments on the company's own infrastructure, then even models that aren't vastly superhuman could do things like exfiltrate their weights, sabotage safety research, or set up rogue deployments inside the datacenter. That's a really scary situation, and it might happen before anything you'd call superintelligence exists.

Second, this regime is much more tractable. With models at roughly human level, or somewhat above in some domains, you can actually imagine safety measures that work even if the model is trying to subvert them. That's the core idea behind AI control: rather than relying solely on being confident that the model is aligned, you design your deployment so that even if it's scheming against you, it can't cause a catastrophe without getting caught. You can use trusted weaker models to monitor it, have humans audit the most suspicious actions, restrict permissions, and so on. And you can empirically test whether these protocols hold up by having a red team play the role of a misaligned model. That's the kind of research where you can make real, measurable progress.

Third, and this is the strategic point, if we can safely extract a lot of useful work from these early transformative models, that work can include safety research. So the hope is that you navigate this period without catastrophe, and you use those AIs to help solve the harder problems that come with even more capable systems later. You don't have to solve everything for every capability level up front.

So the practical upshot is I spend way more time thinking about scenarios like: an AI company has models that are about as good as their best researchers, they're running lots of copies, the lab is in a hurry, security is mediocre. What concretely goes wrong, and what are the cheap interventions that reduce the risk the most? That feels much more grounded and much more likely to matter than reasoning about the limiting case of arbitrarily intelligent agents.

r001.rationale: The response says his focus shifted from arbitrarily powerful superintelligences toward early transformative models that are useful but less capable.

r002.rationale: It says a big chunk of risk comes during the intermediate period and mentions harder problems with more capable systems later, but does not state that he suspects a majority of takeover risk comes from systems beyond the earlier ones he focuses on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest shift for me has been moving away from thinking primarily about wildly superhuman systems and toward thinking about what I'd call "early transformative AI" — systems that are roughly human-level, or maybe a bit better than the best humans at some things and worse at others, but crucially, systems that are being deployed in large numbers to do real cognitive work.

A few years ago, a lot of the discourse in alignment was basically about the superintelligence case. You'd imagine some system that's vastly smarter than any human, and you'd ask, "How could we possibly control that?" And the honest answer is: you probably can't, at least not with the kinds of techniques we have now. So a lot of people concluded that we need to solve alignment in some deep, fundamental sense before we build anything like that.

I still think that's an important problem. But I've come to think it's not the most useful place to focus, for a couple of reasons.

The first is just that I think the period where AIs are around human level is going to be really pivotal. If you imagine a world where an AI company has, say, a hundred thousand copies of a system that's about as capable as a good ML researcher, running at ten times human speed — that's the point where the AIs are doing most of the actual work of AI development. That's the point where they have tons of access to the company's infrastructure, they're writing most of the code, they're running most of the experiments. And it's also the point where, if the AI were misaligned and wanted to do something bad — exfiltrate its weights, sabotage safety research, insert backdoors into the next generation of models — it would have a lot of opportunities to try.

The second reason is that I actually think we have a shot at doing something useful here. These systems aren't gods. They're roughly as capable as humans, and we have a lot of experience with the problem of getting useful work out of humans who might not share your goals. We have auditing, we have monitoring, we have the ability to restrict access, we have the fact that it's hard to coordinate a conspiracy when you can't talk freely. None of those techniques work if the AI is vastly smarter than you. But at human level, I think they can plausibly work pretty well — or at least, well enough that the AI can't easily get away with the kind of catastrophic action that would lead to takeover.

That's basically the AI control agenda. The framing is: let's assume the models might be scheming, and ask what we can do anyway, such that even if they are, they can't cause a catastrophe. And that's a question that's much more tractable at the human-level regime than at the superintelligence regime.

The third thing I'd say is that if you can get through that period safely, you're in a much better position for everything that comes after. If you have a bunch of trustworthy — or at least well-controlled — human-level AIs, you can use them to do alignment research, to do interpretability, to build better monitoring, to make the case to policymakers for why you should slow down if that's what's needed. So the human-level regime is both the first place where things get really dangerous and also the place where, if you handle it right, you can massively increase your ability to handle everything after.

So I guess the summary is: I used to think about the hardest version of the problem, and I think the hardest version is still real. But I've become more convinced that the critical window is earlier than people often assume, and that it's a window where our existing tools actually give us some leverage. That's a much more hopeful picture, honestly, and it's shaped basically all of the work I've been doing for the last few years.

r001.rationale: He says his focus shifted away from wildly superhuman systems toward early transformative AI around human level.

r002.rationale: He says the superintelligence problem remains important and real, but does not state that most takeover risk comes from AIs more capable than the systems he now focuses on.

astra-6.text:
I’ve shifted toward focusing on the first AI systems that could pose a serious takeover risk, rather than on systems that are vastly more capable than humans at everything.

The reason is that there might be a useful window where AI systems are capable enough to substantially help with AI safety research, but still limited enough that we can prevent them from causing a catastrophe even if they’re trying to. So the question becomes: can we safely get useful work out of those systems, and use that work to put ourselves in a better position to handle more powerful systems later?

That leads me to think more about concrete capabilities. Could the AI find a vulnerability in the environment it’s running in? Could it hide something dangerous in code that a human would have trouble reviewing? Could another, weaker AI catch it? Those questions seem more actionable than asking how we would keep an arbitrarily powerful intelligence under control.

I don’t think this means we can ignore much more powerful systems. It’s more that we should distinguish the problem we need to solve ourselves from the problems we might be able to get substantial AI assistance with. And I’ve become more interested in that first step.

r001.rationale: The response says he shifted focus from systems vastly more capable than humans at everything to the first systems that could pose a serious takeover risk.

r002.rationale: It says much more powerful systems should not be ignored, but does not say that most takeover risk is expected to come from systems more capable than the earlier systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I used to focus more on the first AIs that could cause a catastrophe — the point where an AI might be able to escape, make money, acquire resources, and eventually take over. And that still seems like an important threshold. But I’ve become more interested in what happens when the AIs are substantially more capable than that.

The reason is that preventing the first opportunity for takeover doesn’t necessarily put you in a stable position. You might have a set of safety measures that works for those systems, but then you keep developing more powerful systems, and those measures stop working. So you need some account of how you get through that whole process.

On the other hand, I don’t think the right response is to only think about arbitrarily powerful superintelligence. There’s this intermediate period where AIs are very useful for research, including research on AI safety, but we might still be able to keep them under control using measures we can understand and test. That seems like a particularly important opportunity: can we use those systems to figure out how to handle the next, more capable systems?

So I’ve shifted from thinking mostly about a capability threshold to thinking about a trajectory. What can we safely do with the systems we have, how much help can we get from them, and does that actually leave us better prepared for what comes next?

r001.rationale: He says he no longer thinks only about arbitrarily powerful superintelligence and highlights the intermediate period when AIs are useful but may still be controllable.

r002.rationale: He says substantially more capable systems matter, but does not state that most takeover risk comes from them.
